text: TET-30 — reporting prose that moved while its claims stood still
## What the data can and cannot answer

The ticket's claim that this is computable from data tetel already holds survives contact with the code, and the shape of that data decides most of the design. Prose and claim logs both ship inside the snapshot beside the memo, every event in them is timestamped, and the citation edge a paragraph carries is a field on the prose event itself. Two details the ticket does not mention narrow what can be built. Neither `prose::load_all` nor `claims::load_all` surfaces a timestamp — both replay their log into a struct that keeps only a revision count — so this check reads the JSONL directly rather than reusing the loaded types the rest of `check` works from. And a prose block's id exists only inside the workspace: `compose::render` writes the block's text and its `*cites:` marker and nothing else, so a residue line that says `P4` names something a reader holding only the memo cannot find. Claim ids do not have that problem — the rendered ledger prints the workspace id verbatim.
## The anchor: first proof, not last pass

The ticket's phrase "the last grounding pass" is not merely ambiguous, as the open questions suspected — read literally it is self-defeating, and this is the design's first and largest departure. Every grounding pass is briefed on every claim in the ledger, whether or not it has been graded before, so a pass that finds nothing to change still appends a fresh record against the unchanged wording. The two memos already in this tree show what that produces: one claim carrying ten records on a single unchanged digest, written by three passes across nearly half an hour, and another graded `qualifies` twice by different passes fifteen minutes apart on text nobody touched. Anchor the comparison at the most recent grading and the anchor walks forward every round; fix-round prose written in round three stops being "since the last pass" the moment round four runs, even though no pass has ever read a word of the prose. The trail this residue is named after ran six rounds. So the anchor is the earliest record grading a claim's current wording — the moment that wording first entered proof. A later pass over unchanged text cannot move it, and only a revision of the claim itself, followed by a grading of the new wording, ever does.
## The rule

With the anchor fixed, the rule states itself. A prose block is listed when it is a paragraph rather than a heading, it cites at least one id, every cited id resolves to a ledger claim, every one of those claims is in proof, and the event that set the block's current text is later than the latest of its claims' first proofs. "In proof" is not a new predicate: it is the digest comparison `analyze_ledger` already performs, empty-digest grandfathering included, reused rather than reinvented. The two quantifier choices the open questions asked about fall out of the anchor rather than being decided by taste. Per claim, take the earliest in-proof record, because that is when the wording settled. Per block, take the latest of those, because a block is not anchored until all of its evidence base has settled — taking the earliest instead would list every paragraph whose text merely postdates its first-graded citation, which is nearly all of them. Against the two memos already in this tree the rule lists nothing, and the reason it lists nothing is the reason to trust it: each of their post-grounding prose edits either accompanied a claim revision, which moves that claim's first proof past the edit, or touched a heading. Reconstruct the shape it exists for — move one tet29 paragraph ten minutes past the last first proof and touch no claim — and it lists that paragraph alone.

On the first open question — creation or revision — the residue is about neither act specifically but about the text's age: the timestamp used is whichever event set the block's current wording. The exposure is the same in both directions, since a paragraph written fresh under already-graded claims rests on them exactly as ungradedly as a rewritten one, and the ticket's own vector could have arrived either way. What makes the choice cheap rather than merely principled is that counting creations adds almost no listings. A paragraph written in a fix round to carry a new assertion normally cites a new claim, and a new claim is not yet in proof; once a pass puts it in proof, that first proof is later than the paragraph, so the block never becomes listable at all. The creations that do get listed are the ones worth listing: new paragraphs resting on nothing but old, settled claims.

Anchoring at first proof has a second consequence worth stating on its own, because it is what keeps the line from becoming a formality. A further grounding pass over unchanged wording appends records but cannot move the earliest one, so no amount of re-grounding clears a listed block — which is right, since a grounding pass never reads the prose and could not vouch for it if it did. Two things clear it: reverting the text, or revising a cited claim (or adding one) and having the new wording graded. That second remedy is precisely what the finding asks for, because the defect being surfaced is prose asserting something no claim carries. The cost is that there is no cheap discharge. A flow-only edit made after a memo's claims have settled stays listed until some claim moves, and a memo shipped with such an edit ships the line with it. That is a smaller version of a bill this project has paid badly before — the `no scope declared` line once printed once per claim, burying findings about the document under a constant — but it differs in the two ways that matter: it is about this document rather than about tetel, and it names concrete acts that clear it.
## The cross-process comparison, and the digest-shaped alternative that does not exist

The third open question is the one that deserved its suspicion, and it does not dissolve. This would be the first check to order two events recorded by different processes, and the ordering is sound in unit but not in clock. Both timestamps come from a `now_unix` that is byte-identical in the only two places the worktree defines it, so they are the same epoch and the same unit with no timezone term between them; what nothing in either record establishes is that the two processes read the same wall clock. The bound that follows is exact, and the design's position is that it must be printed rather than left implicit: a reported ordering can be wrong only if the grounding process's clock differed from the authoring workspace's by more than the interval between the prose edit and the pass that first put the cited claims in proof. Choosing first proof over last pass is what makes that interval a grounding round rather than seconds in the case this residue exists for — but nothing measured here bounds it from below, and no claim is made that it is always large.

So the question becomes whether the digest-shaped alternative the open question hoped for exists, and in the sharp sense it does not — for a structural reason, not an oversight. `out_of_proof` can compare digests because a record carries a digest of the very text it graded. No record names or digests a prose block anywhere in its shape, and the brief a pass receives is id, proposition and pin. Putting a prose digest into a record would mean the grounding pass reading the prose it exists to grade blind, which trades the independence the whole loop is built on for a residue line. A weaker alternative is genuinely constructible and was worked through rather than waved away: `render --out` could append a publication record — each prose block's text digest, each claim's proposition digest and whether anything grades it — and the residue would then be an ordinal comparison between successive publications with no clock in it at all. It is rejected on resolution. A publication log samples only at the renders an author happens to perform, so a grading and a prose edit falling inside one interval are indistinguishable — and the shape this residue is named after (a pass, then fix-round prose, then one render) lies entirely inside a single interval. The clock-free formulation would have missed the finding it was built for. That is the trade, stated plainly: the timestamp comparison buys the one ordering that matters and pays for it with a bound it prints.

The vacuous case needs no special handling, because the in-proof gate already does the work, and the reason it is the right gate is non-overlap rather than convenience. A claim with no records is already printed as ungrounded; a claim whose records all grade superseded text is already a machine failure as out of proof. A paragraph resting on either is therefore already in front of the reader under a line that says something truer about it than this one could. Requiring every cited claim to be in proof means a memo with no evidence ledger, and a memo halfway through its first draft, lists nothing — the residue is empty until the memo has been graded, which is exactly when it becomes capable of saying anything. Two populations sit outside the rule. Headings, which cite nothing by construction, and paragraphs that cite nothing by choice. The second is a real gap: an uncited paragraph is the one place a false assertion can sit with no citation edge to compare it against, and that belongs in the printed non-coverage list rather than in a footnote here.
## What the reader sees

The last open question asks whether this is a line or a section, and the answer is neither exactly: it is bullets in the flat human-owed list, one per listed block, with a single preamble bullet ahead of them. There are no sub-headings in that partition today, so a section would be the only one and would announce by its shape that it outranks everything beside it. The preamble carries the one thing constant across the entries — that the ordering rests on two clocks nothing here can prove are the same — and it is printed once rather than per bullet for the reason this crate already recorded when it collapsed `no scope declared` to a single document-level line: repeating a constant per row buries the findings that are actually about the document. Each entry names the block's workspace id and the line in this document where its text begins, because a block's id is never written into the rendered output and an id alone points at something the reader cannot find; that mapping comes from one new function in `compose`, consumed by `render`, so the block-to-line correspondence is described once. The entry then names each cited claim with its first-proof timestamp and the pass that wrote it, and the block's own timestamp — the inputs to the comparison, printed so a reader can disagree with the conclusion rather than having to trust it.
## Implementation surface, and what it deliberately does not catch

Everything the implementer touches is declared in the modification-target section above, and there are six symbols: a field on `Findings`; a new `prose_after_proof` that computes the list from the snapshot's prose and claim logs plus the evidence records `check_file` has already loaded; the call to it inside `check_file`'s existing snapshot block, beside the other findings that only exist when a snapshot shipped; a `block_offsets` in `compose` that `render` consumes; the print loop and one added clause in the human-owed scope sentence; and the new `NON_COVERAGE` entries. `machine_check_failed` is untouched, which is what makes the line human-owed by construction rather than by good intentions. Nothing new ships in the snapshot, because both logs this reads are already in it; no schema changes; nothing is executed and no file the document names is opened, so `check`'s standing guarantees hold unchanged. Without a snapshot the list is simply not computed, in silence, exactly as the note-versus-extent check and the mint windows are not, and the bullet that already reports a missing snapshot explains why. Four things go into the printed non-coverage list. False prose that ships alongside a claim revision, which the ticket concedes and this design does not fix. A paragraph that cites nothing, which has no edge to compare against at all. Whether the two clocks agree. And whether the prose is wrong, which nothing here judges and nothing here should.

One thing worth settling explicitly, because both sibling tickets in this family had to be reformulated over it: TET-30 does not share their problem, and not by luck. Their triggers required deciding from English that a memo was in scope — that it recommended a modification, or that a fix transplanted a mechanism — and both had to be replaced by author declarations. This trigger reads no English. The citation edge is a field the author set with `--cites`, and the ordering is two integers taken off two event logs; the rule was executed end to end over both shipped memos' logs without inspecting a character of prose or proposition text. What stays undecidable is the verdict rather than the trigger: whether a listed paragraph really does assert something its claims do not carry. That is not narrowed, hinted at or scored here. It goes whole to the reader, which is what the human-owed partition is — the one whose own opening sentence ends "none of this is settled by a passing check".
## The vacuous case, and what falls outside the rule

One measurement made in passing deserves recording, because the next ticket in this family will meet it. Declaring these six targets required six whole-worktree searches, and a census captures its entire output into a fact that ships in the snapshot. This repository's previous two snapshots hold whole file dumps on single JSON lines, the longest 57110 bytes, so a search for a symbol this crate discusses re-captures those dumps: `render` came back as 486 matching lines and 405019 characters, `NON_COVERAGE` as 35 lines and 98828, `Findings` as 23 lines and 59.2 KB, against `check_file`'s 5 lines and 285 bytes. Two things follow. The larger captures exceeded what the authoring surface returns, so the symbol populations were established by the searches while their individual sites went unread here — the census fixes rooting and extent, never that anyone inspected each site, which is a thing the census's own non-coverage list already says in another form. And the cost compounds: every memo added under `docs/design/` enlarges the next memo's census of any symbol it discusses.

Every observation in this memo was taken against the tetel repository at commit e19a4694bedd1bd2bda91626362f9c2d05f35274 ("transplant: select the donor's premises, and answer each one"), so the TET-28 census and the TET-29 premise inventory are both present in the tree this design reads, as shipped code rather than as sibling proposals. TET-30 asks for one human-owed residue line in `check`: the prose blocks revised since the last grounding pass whose cited claims were not. Not a refusal, no judgement about whether the prose is wrong, and computed rather than authored. This memo settles what the anchor is, which timestamps are compared and across what, what the rule does with a memo nothing has graded, what the reader sees, and what the whole thing cannot see.

The answer, up front. The ticket's mechanism is buildable and its data is all present, but its anchor is wrong in a way that would have made it silent on the very finding it cites: "since the last grounding pass" walks forward every round, because every pass is briefed on every claim and re-grades unchanged wording, so fix-round prose stops being recent as soon as another round runs. The anchor is therefore the earliest record grading a claim's current wording — the moment that wording first entered proof — and a block is listed when its text postdates the latest such moment among the claims it cites, with every one of those claims required to be in proof. That single change settles the ticket's other ambiguities as side effects: it decides earliest-versus-latest in both quantifiers, it makes the vacuous cases empty without a special rule, it makes creation and revision the same question, and it makes the line unclearable by a pass that never read the prose. What it does not remove is a cross-process clock comparison, which no digest-shaped alternative can replace, because no evidence record has anywhere to put a digest of prose and the pass that would compute one is required not to read it. That bound is printed, once, above the entries it qualifies.

text: What clears a listing is the whole design, and it took two refutations to get right. Start with what is easy: a further grounding pass over unchanged wording appends records but cannot move the earliest one, so no amount of re-grounding clears a block — which is correct, since a grounding pass never reads the prose and could not vouch for it if it did. The first refutation was that reverting a paragraph could not clear it either. Prose history is append-only, so a revert appends a later timestamp; keyed on the last event, restoring the settled wording would have left the listing standing forever. Looking the timestamp up by content rather than by event order fixes that. The second refutation is sharper and came from attacking the fix. Keyed on text alone, an author could leave the text untouched and revise only the citations — an act `prose::revise` does not even inspect, and one the `cite` parameter was added to permit — pointing the paragraph at some claim the fix round had legitimately revised and regraded. The anchor moved forward, the timestamp stayed frozen, the line went out, and the machine partition stayed green. A residue that can be silenced by an act indistinguishable from good authoring is worse than no residue, because it certifies. Keying the timestamp on the text and the citation list together closes it: change either and the timestamp moves with it. A third construction closed with it — an old uncited paragraph handed a citation to an already-settled claim, which under the earlier rule entered the list with a timestamp predating everything and was permanently unlistable. So two things clear a listing: restoring the text and citations the claims settled under, and revising or adding a cited claim and having the new wording graded. The second is precisely what the finding asks for, because the defect being surfaced is prose asserting something no claim carries. The cost is that neither is cheap. A flow-only edit made after a memo's claims have settled stays listed until some claim moves or the edit is undone, and a memo shipped with such an edit ships the line with it. That is a smaller version of a bill this project has paid badly before — the `no scope declared` line once printed once per claim, burying findings about the document under a constant — but it differs in the two ways that matter: it is about this document rather than about tetel, and it names concrete acts that clear it.

text: The vacuous case needs no special handling, because the in-proof test already does the work — but which test turned out to matter, and attack decided it rather than argument. It is not the same reader service — `ungrounded: C99` is a line about a claim, not about the paragraph — and worse, it made adding a record-less citation a way to silence any listing at all, with a clean machine partition, since a claim with no records is human-owed rather than out of proof. So the test is existential: one in-proof citation is enough to anchor a block, and a record-less citation contributes nothing to the anchor and cannot suppress anything. Non-overlap survives for what is still skipped — a block every one of whose citations is ungrounded or out of proof is already reported, under `ungrounded` or under a machine failure. Two populations remain outside the rule entirely. Headings, which cite nothing by construction, and paragraphs that cite nothing by choice. text: Everything the implementer touches is declared in the modification-target section above, and there are six symbols: a field on `Findings`; a new `prose_after_proof`; the call to it inside `check_file`'s existing snapshot block, beside the other findings that only exist when a snapshot shipped; a `block_offsets` in `compose` that `render` consumes; the print loop and one added clause in the human-owed scope sentence; and the new `NON_COVERAGE` entries. The check has two inputs: the snapshot's `prose.jsonl`, read directly because the loader discards timestamps, and the claims and evidence `check_file` already holds. text: So the question becomes whether the digest-shaped alternative the ticket hoped for exists. Two were examined; both fail, and no claim is made that a third could not be found. The sharp one — a record carrying a digest of the prose it vouches for, the exact analogue of `out_of_proof` — cannot be built, for a structural reason rather than an oversight. `out_of_proof` compares digests because a record carries a digest of the very text it graded. No record names or digests a prose block anywhere in its shape, and the brief a pass receives is id, proposition and pin. Putting a prose digest into a record would mean the grounding pass reading the prose it exists to grade blind, which trades the independence the whole loop is built on for a residue line. The weaker one is genuinely constructible and was worked through rather than waved away: `render --out` could append a publication record — each prose block's text digest, each claim's proposition digest and whether anything grades it — and the residue would then be an ordinal comparison between successive publications with no clock in it at all. It is rejected on resolution. A publication log samples only at the renders an author happens to perform, so a grading and a prose edit falling inside one interval are indistinguishable — and the shape this residue is named after (a pass, then fix-round prose, then one render) lies entirely inside a single interval. The clock-free formulation would have missed the finding it was built for. That is the trade, stated plainly: the timestamp comparison buys the one ordering that matters and pays for it with a bound it prints.
why: C8 was narrowed after attack pass a1 declined to treat it as exhaustive: it attacked two axes and says so. The paragraph read as though every clock-free formulation had been ruled out.

text: The answer, up front. Every input this design needs is present in data tetel already ships, so the mechanism is buildable — but the ticket's anchor is wrong in a way that would have made it silent on the very finding it cites. "Since the last grounding pass" walks forward every round, because every pass is briefed on every claim and re-grades unchanged wording, so fix-round prose stops being recent as soon as another round runs. The anchor is therefore the earliest record grading a claim's current wording — the moment that wording first entered proof — and a block is listed when its text postdates the latest such moment among the claims it cites that are in proof. That single change settles the ticket's other ambiguities as side effects: it decides earliest-versus-latest in both quantifiers, it empties the vacuous cases without a special rule, it makes creation and revision the same question, and it stops a grounding pass from blessing prose it never read. Two smaller corrections were forced by attack rather than reached by design, and both are on the other side of the comparison. A block's timestamp is looked up by its text *and* its citation list together, not by its last event: keyed on the event, restoring a paragraph's settled wording could never clear the line, and keyed on text alone, a citation-only revision could silence one in seconds using a claim the fix round had legitimately produced. And the in-proof test is existential, because requiring every citation to be in proof let a single record-less citation suppress a block with nothing red to show for it. What none of this removes is a cross-process clock comparison, which neither digest-shaped alternative examined here can replace, because no evidence record has anywhere to put a digest of prose and the pass that would compute one is required not to read it. That bound is printed once, in a preamble above the entries it qualifies.

text: One property is worth settling explicitly, because it is where a rule of this family usually goes wrong: the trigger interprets no English. It is not keyed on deciding from a memo's prose that the memo is in scope. The citation edge is a field the author set with `--cites`, the heading flag is a boolean on the same event, and the ordering is a comparison of integers taken off two logs. Text is consumed in exactly two places, and both are byte comparisons. The in-proof test feeds a claim's proposition into sha256; and finding a block's text timestamp means testing each of its past versions for equality with the current text and citation list, which reads every version of every paragraph as bytes. Nothing anywhere parses a sentence, matches a phrase, or forms a view about what a paragraph is about. What stays undecidable is the verdict rather than the trigger: whether a listed paragraph really does assert something its claims do not carry. That is not narrowed, hinted at or scored here. It goes whole to the reader, which is what the human-owed partition is — the one whose own opening sentence ends "none of this is settled by a passing check".
why: C12 was corrected after k2 refuted "the one place text is consumed at all": the timestamp lookup is a second byte comparison over prose text. The paragraph carried the single-place claim.

text: One measurement made in passing deserves recording, because the next ticket in this family will meet it. Declaring these six targets required six whole-worktree searches, and a census captures its entire output into a fact that ships in the snapshot. This repository's previous two snapshots hold whole file dumps on single JSON lines — tet29's longest is 57249 bytes, tet28's 34477 — so a search for a symbol this crate discusses re-captures those dumps. What such a search costs turns out to be a property of the instrument and the moment rather than of the symbol, in two separate ways. Scope: `render` matches 486 lines and 373271 bytes of this tree in the state the census was taken in, or 447 and 311672 with `.git/` and `target/` excluded as well; `NON_COVERAGE` 35 and 95637, `Findings` 23 and 57418, `check_file` 5 and 285, and the two symbols that do not exist yet nothing at all. Those numbers hold still because the trees they range over are frozen. Time: the same counts taken with this memo's own artifacts included do not hold still at all. `render` measured 529 lines and 1136689 bytes at one point in this memo's review and 550 and 1202134 later, with no source change in between — what grew was this memo's evidence log, now 59 records and 164392 bytes, and its snapshot, whose longest fact line is the 574898-byte capture of the `render` census itself. Grading a claim about census cost enlarges the thing the claim is about, which is the compounding thesis demonstrating itself. What survives both is the ordering and the direction: censusing a symbol this crate talks about costs orders of magnitude more than censusing one it does not, and every memo added under `docs/design/` enlarges the next memo's census of anything it discusses.
why: C13 was corrected after k2 found its "once they exist" figures already stale — grading the claim had grown this memo's own evidence log — and its 57110 figure to be characters rather than bytes. The paragraph quoted both.
